facts.claim: Modern digital cues can hijack attentional resources even when they are not personally relevant.
facts.quote: Together, our results show that modern digital cues can hijack attentional resources, even in the absence of explicit personal relevance.

facts.claim: Technology companies use psychological cues to design digital experiences that capture people's attention.
facts.quote: Our study showed that technology companies employ psychological cues to design digital experiences that capture individuals' attention.

facts.claim: Social media notifications are linked to changes in pupil dilation, which is a physiological marker of cognitive load.
facts.quote: These findings were mirrored in changes in pupil dilation, a physiological marker of cognitive load, confirming the convergent impact of notification relevance and smartphone habits.

facts.claim: Neuroimaging tests confirmed that participants experienced a dopamine response when they received alerts.
facts.quote: Neuroimaging tests confirmed the dopamine response participants experienced when they received alerts, which is why it is hard to change these habits.

facts.claim: 29.8% of students and working professionals reported they could not focus on their work or engage in proper interactions.
facts.quote: 29. 8% of students and working professionals reported they could not focus on their work or engage in proper interactions.

facts.claim: A study of Indians between the ages of 15 to 35 found a moderate to severe case of nomophobia.
facts.quote: The purpose of this study is to ascertain the degree of nomophobia among Indians between the ages of 15 to 35. ... there is a serious concern for our "physical, mental, and social health" and a moderate to severe case of nomophobia

research.angle: While technology companies use psychological cues and alerts to trigger dopamine responses and hijack attention, the evidence focuses more on the resulting cognitive load and habits than on specific variable reward schedules.
research.verdict: The sources confirm that notifications trigger dopamine and hijack attention, but they do not explicitly link these mechanisms to gambling-style variable reward schedules.
research.caveat: One source regarding the hijacking of attention is a preprint and has not yet been peer reviewed.
